title: Time
tomorrow: one tap to check the essay prompt, and now it's 1:40 a.m. how?

cards: A phone counts time without a sound, which may be why a whole evening can slip away without one. An old wall clock does it out loud: every second, a click.

The letter to the Ephesians has a phrase for getting some of those clicks back: “Redeeming the time, because the days are evil.” Redeem, as in buy back, the way someone pays to get a thing out of a pawnshop.
So what does it cost to buy back an hour?

teach.b: Here's the whole sentence: “See then that ye walk circumspectly, not as fools, but as wise, Redeeming the time, because the days are evil.” Circumspectly means looking around as you walk, eyes open.
The days are evil isn't a reason to panic; it's a reason not to drift. Time doesn't buy itself back.

teach.h: TEACH US TO NUMBER OUR DAYS.
teach.b: A psalm asks for the skill: “So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom.” Counting days isn't gloomy. It makes them audible, the way a ticking clock makes a minute something you can hear.

And Ecclesiastes keeps this from turning into frantic busyness: “To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven.” A time to work, and a time to sit on a porch doing nothing much.
So redeeming the time doesn't mean filling every minute.
It means paying for some of them on purpose, with attention, and handing them to what lasts: prayer, scripture, a visit to someone lonely, worship with others, a long walk.
Christians spend that hour in different ways. The price is the same for everyone: something else doesn't get it.

how: Christians mark time with the church year, Sunday worship and daily prayer; some set aside a regular hour each week for prayer, scripture or visiting someone who is lonely.

o: the hours you owe to your work and nothing else
an endless supply that's yours to spend later
the days you're given, some bought back on purpose

games.q: buying back time — tap the pairs.

s: redeeming the time means filling every minute
Ecclesiastes gives every thing a season, rest and porches included.
Ephesians gives its reason in the same breath: the days are evil
redeeming the time, because the days are evil: a reason not to drift.
the psalm calls counting your days a gloomy habit
it asks to be taught to number our days, to gain a heart of wisdom.

games.q: a canceled practice frees up saturday morning. by Ephesians, what does redeeming that time look like?
o: choose one hour on purpose for something that lasts, and rest the rest.
fill every minute with productive tasks, so none of it is wasted.
plan nothing at all; time can't really be bought back.
games.why: redeeming the time is buying some hours back on purpose, not filling every minute: there's a season for rest too.

practice: Find one steady sound near you: a clock, a fan, the hum of a fridge, or your own breath if the room is quiet. Listen to it for the whole sit, and let each beat be one moment you are actually there for.
Before you finish, choose one hour this week to give to something that lasts.

wordCard.voice: Time. The days you're given, numbered and not endless, some of them bought back on purpose.

orig.note: the Greek in Ephesians 5:16 behind 'redeeming': buying up, buying back.
